$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 9 \\ 9 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 9 \\ 9 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 9 \\ 9 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) \\ 4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)\,c$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(0)=c$  

$\text{L6}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,x(0)$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ is obtained from the defining initial value problem for ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ by  
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by  
{{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is a fundamental matrix for the system, every solution can be written as 

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c\,\text{for some constant vector }c.
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{properties of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider line $\text{L4}.$ The standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is defined as the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

The second condition, ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},$ is exactly line $\text{L4}.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ is obtained from the defining initial value problem for ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ by $\text{using the initial condition }{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ From line $\text{L3}$ we have

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

and from line $\text{L4}$ we know ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.$ Replacing ${Φ}_{0}(0)$ with ${I}_{n}$ in the equation $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c$ gives

$$
x(0)={I}_{n}c=c,
$$

which is exactly line $\text{L5}.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by $\text{replacing }{Φ}_{0}(0)\text{ with }{I}_{n}\text{ in }x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c.$

Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$  

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L6}$ by
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Line $\text{L5}$ gives

$$
({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c.
$$

Since $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}={I}_{n}$, the right-hand side simplifies to $c$, so

$$
c=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0}).
$$

Simplify once, then apply $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}$, to obtain

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L6}.$ Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L6}$, and $\text{L7}.$ From $\text{L3}$ we have

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c.
$$

Using $\text{L6}$, we substitute $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})$ to obtain

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L7}.$ Thus, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L6}$ by $\text{substituting }c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\text{ into }x(t)={e}^{At}c.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Since $At$ and $-A{t}_{0}$ commute, we can combine the exponentials:

$$
{e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}.
$$

Substituting this into line $\text{L7}$ gives line $\text{L8}.$ Thus, line $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by $\text{the fact that }{e}^{X}{e}^{Y}={e}^{X+Y}\text{ when }X\text{ and }Y\text{ commute}.$
